item.title: Anthropic releases a shorter Lean 4 formal verification of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions based on Claude's proof
item.description: Anthropic has published a Lean 4 formal proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) for Dirichlet L-functions, building on Levent Alpöge's work and using Claude, their AI assistant. The repository includes two editions: a readable version with about 300,000 lines and a compact version with about 76,000 lines, both requiring Lean v4.35.0 and Mathlib for building. The proof has passed machine verification but has not yet been reviewed by mathematicians or accompanied by a formal paper.

item.title: OpenAI corrects GPT-6.2 billing error, increasing Astra usage limits by 40% and Sol by 25%, adds banked reset for affected users [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI acknowledged a billing mistake at the launch of GPT-6.2 that had incorrectly discounted usage for Astra and Sol models, causing users to consume their plan allowances faster than intended. The company fixed the error, resulting in users reaching their limits 40% faster on GPT-6.2 Astra and 25% faster on Sol compared to last week, though these models still offer more usage than previous versions. Other models were unaffected, and OpenAI will not charge users retroactively for the difference. As compensation, OpenAI is providing one banked reset to all users on Go, Plus, Pro, and Business plans.

item.title: Researchers build ASTERISM, a large multi-image benchmark revealing multimodal LLMs often rely on single-image shortcuts, and propose cross-image credit assignment to improve training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers audited 33,000 items from 19 public multi-image benchmarks and found that 24.2% can be answered using only one image or the question alone, leading multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to take a single-image shortcut even when multiple images are needed. They created ASTERISM, the largest audited multi-image benchmark with 18,700 items requiring multiple images, along with training and hard subsets. The strongest proprietary MLLM scored 68% on the hardest subset. The study found that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), commonly used in MLLM post-training, inadvertently rewards this shortcut because correct answers from one image receive the same reward as those combining multiple images. To address this, the researchers proposed cross-image credit assignment (CICA), an extension of RLVR that shifts credit toward tokens requiring multiple images. Applying CICA to three open-source MLLMs improved ASTERISM scores by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than doubling gains from other reinforcement learning objectives trained on the same data.

item.title: Researchers introduce Actionwave, a benchmark for waveform-centric clinical prediction across ICU, operating room, and emergency settings, comparing models on 20 tasks with 1.4 million labeled windows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Actionwave is a new benchmark designed to evaluate clinical prediction models that use continuous bedside waveform data across intensive care, operating room, and emergency department scenarios. It standardizes prediction tasks by decision time and clinical inference goals, varying conditions such as warning time before interventions to reflect real clinical use. The benchmark compares diverse model architectures and pretrained biosignal encoders under fixed model size and compute constraints, using patient-level data splits and strict information cutoffs to isolate modeling factors. The study includes over 87,000 model fits across 20 tasks derived from source datasets totaling 1.4 million labeled windows. Results highlight the importance of task-specific model choices and demonstrate why matched cohorts, unimodal controls, and explicit timing are critical for interpreting waveform model performance in clinical prediction.

item.title: LEGOSpec framework decomposes and optimizes speculative draft models for large language model acceleration, improving acceptance length by up to 34.7% on long-context workloads [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: LEGOSpec is a composable framework designed to improve speculative decoding in large language models by breaking down draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components within a unified training system. The framework systematically evaluates component effects and interactions, revealing that different workloads benefit from tailored backbones, proposal designs must balance acceptance and latency, and training objectives should optimize token distribution matching and acceptance length. Using these insights, the authors developed DFlux, a general-purpose draft model combining a hybrid backbone, residual corrector, and hierarchical supervision, which outperforms previous baselines by up to 13.7% on standard benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context tasks across Qwen and Gemma models. LEGOSpec also enhances training efficiency through metadata-aware scheduling and asynchronous execution, boosting throughput by up to 79% and speeding offline supervision preparation by over three times compared to prior methods.

item.title: Researchers introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy trained on one million robot designs to adapt behavior to diverse robot kinematics and achieve high task success [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OmniAct is a manipulation policy that conditions on each robot's kinematic graph to produce embodiment-specific behavior, enabling control across robots with varying degrees of freedom and configurations. The researchers procedurally generated and filtered one million physically feasible robot embodiments, developed algorithms to simulate trajectories for all, and trained OmniAct on diverse manipulation tasks. In evaluations on 2,000 held-out embodiment-scene pairs, OmniAct achieved a 63.0% success rate, outperforming baselines and showing nearly double the success on a previously unseen real-world robot compared to the next best method. The policy learns distinct manipulation strategies that leverage each robot's unique morphology and capabilities.

item.title: Researchers introduce CogLoadBench to measure extraneous cognitive load effects on large language models across reasoning tasks and propose Extraneous Load Score to estimate and mitigate load impact [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed CogLoadBench, a benchmark designed to isolate and measure extraneous cognitive load effects on large language models (LLMs) by varying presentation factors across reasoning tasks. They found that higher extraneous load often reduces model accuracy by increasing competition or complicating reasoning paths. To address this, they propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a metric computed from model activations that estimates extraneous load and generalizes across tasks and load levels. The study also demonstrates that adjusting model representations toward lower-load directions during inference can improve performance without altering prompt content.

item.title: Researchers analyze dependency-ready decoding in masked diffusion language models, finding limited benefits beyond left-to-right decoding and questioning reliance on attention mechanisms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have demonstrated strong performance on structured reasoning tasks by allowing flexible token unmasking orders. Researchers examined the principle of dependency-ready decoding, which prioritizes resolving token dependencies before unmasking, to assess its impact on accuracy from both practical and theoretical perspectives. They found that decoders implementing dependency readiness through attention often revert to left-to-right decoding when outperforming confidence-based methods. Theoretical analysis introduced an information-theoretic measure of dependency and showed that when prediction margins are large, maximum-margin decoding already commits to dependency-ready tokens, limiting the scope for future dependency-ready decoders. These findings suggest that the potential advantage of dependency-ready decoding is confined to cases with small margins and that reliance on attention for this purpose should be reconsidered.

item.title: Researchers present closed-form weight-space programming using LLM-written classifiers on a frozen RoBERTa-large encoder, matching or exceeding gradient fine-tuning on multiple datasets without updating encoder weights [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce closed-form weight-space programming (WSP), where a large language model writes programs that fit classifiers on a frozen masked language model using cloze-style prompts and closed-form methods, avoiding gradient computation and encoder updates. Evaluated on RoBERTa-large across 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 labels, WSP outperforms full fine-tuning and LoRA at all label budgets and approaches prompt-based fine-tuning performance, especially excelling in low-label regimes. On six held-out datasets, WSP remains competitive, consistently outperforming LoRA and staying close to full fine-tuning, though prompt-based fine-tuning leads with large label counts. The method is deterministic, requires multiple encoder passes per template, and the study reports extensive experimental details including unsuccessful approaches.

item.title: Researchers introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 human-written puzzles with community-verified answers from Puzzling Stack Exchange, to evaluate nine language models including GPT-6.1 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Puzzling-Bench comprises a diverse set of puzzles such as riddles, ciphers, logic grids, and recreational mathematics, with about one-third including images. Each puzzle includes the author's accepted answer, hints, community tags, and creation dates, enabling detailed analysis and contamination checks against model training data. Nine advanced language models were evaluated using a two-tier scoring system combining exact match and LLM judgment, with GPT-6.1 achieving the highest accuracy of 74.8% on a shared subset of 255 puzzles. A core set of 17 puzzles defeated all models, and an oracle ensemble reached 91% accuracy. A multimodal pilot showed that withholding images reduced model performance significantly. The dataset, scoring pipeline, and provenance data have been publicly released for further research.

item.title: Researchers introduce CARE-OPD to improve on-policy distillation efficiency for long-horizon agents, boosting task success by 59.5% and cutting training time by 45% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: CARE-OPD (Collect for coverAge, Replay with Evidence) addresses limitations in fully online on-policy distillation (OPD) for long-horizon agents by expanding history coverage and filtering unreliable updates through student-seeded teacher completions and confidence gating. It also uses hindsight replay allocation to focus on critical decisions during trajectory reuse. Evaluated on long-horizon tasks in software engineering and deep research, CARE-OPD outperforms existing OPD and prefix replay methods, significantly improving task success rates while reducing training time and environment interactions.

item.title: PersonaFactory generates over 740,000 synthetic user personas and 1.24 million persona-styled conversations in 85 languages to augment AI training prompts with stylistic diversity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: PersonaFactory is an end-to-end pipeline that creates detailed synthetic user personas to augment existing user prompts, addressing the lack of stylistic variation in out-of-the-box large language model outputs. It produces a large bank of structured personas and a corpus of persona-styled conversations, enabling more natural and diverse user-AI interactions across multiple languages. The system uses attribute-based style representations to control style adoption and preserve user intent better than free-text persona descriptions, as evaluated by automated metrics and human experts. PersonaFactory's augmented conversations perform comparably to original training data on capability benchmarks and adapt reply styles more closely to users without explicit steering, improving assistant persona control in AI training.

item.title: Researchers propose DART method to generate diverse alternative reasoning traces for hard math problems, improving problem recovery by 37% over Monte Carlo sampling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a method that starts from rejected reasoning traces in large language models and generates distinct alternative reasoning steps to solve difficult math problems. DART ranks uncertain reasoning steps and produces alternative candidates guided by reference answers and meta-thoughts, enhancing problem-solving coverage. On the DeepMath-103K dataset, DART recovers 37% more problems than independent Monte Carlo sampling at the same number of generated traces, with a 30% lower cost per accepted trace. Post-training the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model on DART-mined traces yields top performance in five out of six evaluations on MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks, demonstrating DART's effectiveness in expanding problem coverage and improving training data quality for mathematical reasoning tasks.

item.title: Researchers find semantic density metrics do not predict memory collapse in LLM agents across multiple task environments
item.description: Researchers evaluated 14 memory-store statistics, including mean pairwise cosine similarity, across 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods in various task environments to determine if these metrics could warn of declining task accuracy in large language model (LLM) agents. They found no statistic reliably predicted early accuracy decline, with global semantic density measures failing to provide warnings and local crowding metrics not transferring consistently across memory designs. Classifiers trained on this data falsely flagged many stable checkpoints and missed most accuracy drops in extended task runs. The study also observed that size-limited memory stores remained stable over long horizons, while failures occurred only when unbounded whole-store prompting exceeded model input capacity, which was directly predicted by token growth.

item.title: Researchers develop supervised learning confidence scores to improve gating of large language model automation, outperforming baselines on a 2B-parameter model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a supervised learning approach to generate reliable confidence scores for large language model (LLM) outputs, addressing the challenge of LLMs producing incorrect answers with high confidence. Their method fits a linear confidence score head to the final-layer hidden state of a frozen 2B-parameter LLM backbone and trains text-only metamodels for closed models, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain answers for human review. The approach was evaluated on datasets primarily from SQuAD and TruthfulQA, outperforming multiple baselines and metamodels by automating the largest fraction of workload at high accuracy targets. While prompted confidence scores may appear calibrated, they often lack the resolution needed for effective thresholding. The confidence score head showed modest transferability to unseen datasets but remained the most robust method. This framework aims to enhance the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties such as safety or compliance.

item.title: Researchers introduce HumblePRM to improve Vision Language Models' abstention in ambiguous cases by independently scoring perception and calibration stages [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model that enhances Vision Language Models' (VLMs) ability to abstain from confident answers when visual evidence is ambiguous. Unlike standard outcome reward models that only supervise final decisions, HumblePRM separately evaluates the perception stage, where the model describes the scene, and the calibration stage, where it judges if the evidence suffices for a conclusion, rewarding alignment between evidence and expressed confidence. Training with HumblePRM significantly increases abstention on ambiguous inputs without reducing accuracy on clear images, and the improvement also transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger edge model. This approach suggests that process reward supervision can lead to more reliable VLMs with better-calibrated confidence and reduced unpredictable behavior.

item.title: Researchers present vSFT framework to verbally fine-tune language model agents at test time, improving success rates on ALFWorld and WebShop tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT), a framework that enables large language model agents to receive dense natural language feedback and update their weights during test time. The system forms a closed loop where a supervisor generates verbal guidance from failed agent trajectories, and a hypernetwork converts this into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. The vSFT approach using the Qwen3-4B model outperforms existing reinforcement learning methods like GRPO and Reflexion by significant margins in success rates on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks. This method suggests a promising direction for creating agents that can adapt and improve themselves dynamically rather than relying solely on pre-adapted models.

item.title: Researchers propose mismatch-corrected bandits to improve adaptive data sampling by modeling proxy-target model discrepancies, reducing training regret and enhancing worst-group accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers address the problem of proxy models ranking training data differently from target models, which can degrade training performance. They model the mismatch between proxy and target models as a multi-fidelity bandit problem, using rare audits to correct proxy rewards and guide data allocation decisions more effectively. The approach audits uncertain decisions and distributes the audit budget over training to minimize regret. Theoretical analysis proves that proxy-only allocation can lead to linear regret and that a minimum number of paired audits is necessary, with a sliding-window policy achieving improved regret bounds under changing conditions. Experiments on the CivilComments-WILDS dataset demonstrate that mismatch correction improves worst-group accuracy by 6.3 to 10.5 percentage points compared to target-only policies with the same audit budget, validating the method's practical benefits.

item.title: Researchers propose INSPIRE, a two-stage reasoning framework for forecasting emerging entities in temporal knowledge graphs, improving prediction accuracy across ICEWS and GDELT benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce INSPIRE, a two-stage forecasting framework designed to improve reasoning over emerging entities in temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs), which face challenges due to sparse and bursty interaction histories. INSPIRE combines a shared-pattern predictor with an individual-evidence adapter that integrates textual semantic priors and long-range event statistics to enhance prediction accuracy. The framework addresses limitations of existing methods by fusing event-updated memory across candidate catalogs and applying coordinated masking techniques. Evaluations on four benchmarks from ICEWS and GDELT datasets show that INSPIRE significantly improves emerging entity mean reciprocal rank (MRR) by up to 88.83% over strong baselines, with further gains from the individual-evidence adapter. The code for INSPIRE is publicly available for further research and application.

item.title: Researchers introduce token readout-based scoring system and J-lens methods to improve model diffing for backdoor detection in fine-tuned models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present a unified scoring system using token readouts to evaluate weight, activation, and output-based model diffing methods aimed at detecting backdoors introduced during fine-tuning. They enhance existing weight and activation methods by incorporating the J-lens and its refinement, the J++-lens, and test these approaches by comparing backdoored models with their base counterparts. The J++-lens notably improves weight-based detection, ranking backdoor-related tokens among the top ten in most test settings. The study finds that output and activation-based methods like ADL and Diff Mining can fail if the backdoored model is penalized during fine-tuning for assigning probability to backdoor trigger words on clean inputs, whereas weight-based methods remain robust. Conversely, manipulating hidden units or restricting training to certain layers can obscure backdoors from weight-based methods but not from activation or output-based ones. No single method effectively resists all tested evasion techniques, highlighting the challenges in backdoor detection.

item.title: One Model, Many Modes: Evolving System Prompt Ensembles for Creative Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34760v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preference-aligned LLMs can exhibit mode collapse, concentrating their output distributions around a narrow set of high-reward responses. This limits creative generation, which requires quality, novelty, and diversity. Existing test-time methods often emphasize diversity, giving less attention to whether individual responses are both high-quality and novel. This distinction matters in practical use, where users may seek a single compelling, original response. We formalize creative generation as a multi-objective distributional optimization problem and introduce SEPO, a training-free framework for System Prompt Ensemble Optimization. The framework combines prompt evolution with greedy max-min selection to identify behaviorally distinct system prompts under a quality constraint, then uniformly samples one prompt per response at inference time. Across four creative generation tasks with increasing quality requirements and three open-weight models, SEPO ranks first in 8 of 12 settings on the harmonic mean of quality, diversity, and novelty, while no baseline leads in more than two. On average, it raises LLM-judged diversity from 1.92 to 3.43 and novelty from 1.00 to 3.34 over base sampling (1-5 scale), with quality decreasing from 3.72 to 3.30. We further show that expanding the optimized ensemble increases separation among prompt-conditioned response distributions. These results support system prompt ensemble optimization as a promising approach to improving LLM creativity at inference time.

item.title: When Every Rollout Fails: Splicing Learner-Conditioned Options into Long-Horizon Agent RL [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often yields all-fail groups on long-horizon agent tasks: every sampled trajectory receives zero reward, leaving group-relative methods without a reward-based policy gradient. A common remedy supplies complete solutions from a stronger model, but full trajectories are expensive and expose the learner to long off-policy histories. We introduce SPLICE, which constructs local training targets from failed current-policy trajectories online. For each all-fail group, a proposal model selects a splice point in a current-policy trajectory and generates several bounded options from that point. We estimate each option's value using repeated current-policy continuations, convert positive estimates into a return-weighted local target, and fit the current policy on the options. We evaluate SPLICE across two policy families on two long-horizon agent tasks, Software Engineering with SWE-bench Verified and Deep Research with BrowseComp-Plus. SPLICE outperforms GRPO and full-trajectory guidance baselines in all four settings, improving over GRPO by 2.8--9.8 percentage points. On initially failed SWE tasks, it raises GRPO's graduation rate by 10.8 percentage points. Further experiments show that SPLICE improves performance while reducing costly proposal-model computation.

item.title: Explaining Chess and Go with Discovered Motifs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.23166v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern chess engines play far beyond human ability, often choosing moves whose underlying ideas are difficult for humans to understand. We propose an automatic metric for chess explanations based on how well the motifs they describe generalize to new positions. Evaluating state-of-the-art language models using this metric, we find that they perform surprisingly poorly, often relying on surface-level board observations rather than robust, transferable chess concepts. We then introduce BinProp, a training-free method that enables these same models to discover reusable chess concepts and use them to explain moves in natural language. BinProp improves motif generalization for every model tested, nearly tripling the average score compared with direct prompting. Beyond chess, the same method discovers useful concepts in Go, draughts, and shogi without additional tuning.

item.title: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.15735v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.

item.title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.26809v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.

item.title: GDS Agent for Graph Algorithmic Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2508.20637v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable multimodal information processing and reasoning ability. When equipped with tools through function calling and enhanced with retrieval-augmented techniques, compound LLM-based systems can access closed data sources and answer questions about them. However, they still struggle to process and reason over large-scale graph-structure data. In this technical report we introduce the GDS (Graph Data Science) agent. The GDS agent introduces a comprehensive set of graph algorithms as tools, together with preprocessing (retrieval) and postprocessing of algorithm results, in a model context protocol (MCP) server. It is accompanied by a skill that guides the LLM through graph analysis. The agent can be used with any modern LLM out-of-the-box. GDS agent allows users to ask any question that implicitly and intrinsically requires graph algorithmic reasoning about their data, and quickly obtain accurate and grounded answers. We introduce new benchmarks that evaluate intermediate tool calls as well as final responses, and the results indicate that the GDS agent solves a wide spectrum of graph tasks. We also demonstrate how the GDS agent can perform open-ended analyses at the level of domain experts, on tasks such as money laundering tracing and pattern mining in biology. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges and the future roadmap.

item.title: Network of Theseus (like the ship) [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2512.04198v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A standard assumption in deep learning is that the inductive bias introduced by a neural network architecture must persist from training through inference. The architecture you train with is the architecture you deploy. This assumption constrains the community from selecting architectures that may have desirable efficiency or design properties due to difficulties with optimization. We challenge this assumption with the Network of Theseus (NoT), a method for progressively converting a trained, or even untrained, guide network architecture part-by-part into an entirely different target network architecture while preserving the performance of the guide network. At each stage, components in the guide network architecture are incrementally replaced with the target architecture modules and aligned via representational similarity metrics. This procedure preserves most of the functionality of the guide network even under substantial architectural changes-for example, converting a convolutional network into a multilayer perceptron, or GPT-2 into a recurrent neural network. By decoupling optimization from deployment, NoT expands the space of viable inference-time architectures, opening opportunities for better accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs and enabling more directed exploration of the architectural design space.

item.title: Neural Isomorphic Fields: A Transformer-based Algebraic Numerical Embedding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2601.12095v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural network models often face challenges when processing very small or very large numbers due to issues such as overflow, underflow, and unstable output variations. To mitigate these problems, we propose using embedding vectors for numbers instead of directly using their raw values. These embeddings aim to retain essential algebraic properties while preventing numerical instabilities. We introduce Neural Isomorphic Fields (NIF), a digit-sequence Transformer autoencoder trained with two learned commutative operators and an antisymmetric neural comparator. At zero loss, the embeddings provably form an ordered integral domain isomorphic to the decimal fractions, whose field of fractions is isomorphic to the rationals. For the trained model, we bound errors of operations, chains and algebraic laws by decoding margins, defects and Lipschitz constants. Trained on up to 25 digits, NIF reaches at least 99.9% exact match on closure, identity, associativity and distributivity and 99.8% on ten-step chains and the order relation. With four channels per decimal place, reconstruction and both operations exceed 99.7% exact match on numbers of up to 200 digits whose parts stay within training lengths, so the dimension grows linearly. In a language model, frozen operators raise exact match on 14-20-digit word problems from 12.0% (operators off) to 39.7%.

item.title: Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Memory-Efficient Latent Chain-of-Thought with Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2603.21676v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Standard Transformers have a fixed computational depth, limiting their ability to generalize to tasks that require variable-depth reasoning. The usual remedy, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), spends tokens to reason, inflating the key--value cache, so memory becomes the limiting cost when reasoning is served over large query batches. We study a depth-recurrent Transformer that decouples computational depth from parameter count by iterating a shared-weight block, so that adding reasoning steps leaves peak inference memory unchanged and grows latency only linearly, with no token generation. Three ingredients support the recurrence over 20+ thinking steps: a silent thinking objective that supervises only the final output, LayerScale initialization, and an identity-biased gate that opens a gradient highway across steps. We characterize it on three compositional domains with decreasing structural bias: graph reachability (adjacency masking), nested boolean logic (relative positioning), and unstructured relational text (no structural positional cue). We find a \emph{computational frontier}: accuracy climbs once the thinking-step count meets the task's complexity, reaching near-perfect performance on the two structured tasks and a lower plateau on unstructured text. How it climbs depends on the structural bias---abruptly from chance on the graph task, gradually on the other two. Depth recurrence extrapolates beyond the training range: it succeeds on the graph task where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on the two sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth Transformers that use $4$--$6.4\times$ more parameters. On the graph task, whose adjacency mask makes propagation depth verifiable, intermediate per-step supervision---a standard recipe for deep iterative models---consistently \emph{harms} this extrapolation at widths $d \geq 256$. We release the code for reproducibility.

item.title: NSFL: A Post-Training Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzy Logic Framework for Boolean Operators in Neural Embeddings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2604.10604v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Standard dense retrievers have no native mechanism for multi-atom logical constraints. We introduce Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzy Logic (NSFL), a training-free framework that brings fuzzy-logical structure to neural embedding spaces through a first-order finite-difference treatment of similarity. NSFL anchors logical operations on zero-order atomic scores while steering with Neuro-Symbolic Deltas (NS-Delta) -- the marginal semantic contributions induced by contextual fusion -- preserving atomic meaning while capturing contextual dependence, and avoiding the representation collapse and manifold escape endemic to geometric baselines. For latency-constrained deployment, Spherical Query Optimization (SQO) uses Riemannian optimization to project logical formulas into manifold-stable query vectors. Across six encoder configurations and two modalities, NSFL yields mAP@100 improvements up to +81% on QUEST and +70% on a COCO-derived text-to-image benchmark, and provides an additive +19% average gain on an encoder already fine-tuned for logical retrieval. On NevIR, where absolute accuracies are directly interpretable, NSFL doubles pairwise accuracy -- NevIR's both-correct criterion -- from 0.256 to 0.508. The decomposition is exact and general; the operators built on it are engineering realizations rather than a closed algebra, and we state that boundary precisely. Code is available at https://github.com/vladiaidev-lab/NSFL

item.title: Safe Inference-Time Alignment via Lagrangian Reward Augmentation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.02781v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inference-time alignment steers a frozen language model during decoding using auxiliary reward signals, avoiding the cost of repeated weight updates. However, existing inference-time alignment methods typically optimize a single scalar score, so explicit safety constraints must either be ignored or encoded through manually tuned penalties. We propose Lagrangian Reward Augmentation (LARA), a general inference-time alignment framework under safety constraints. Starting from a KL-regularized constrained objective with a reward model and a cost model, LARA dualizes the constraint and reduces the optimization problem to a one-dimensional convex problem over a nonnegative dual variable. Estimated on a small calibration set, this dual variable defines an augmented reward that can be used as a drop-in scoring signal within existing inference-time alignment methods. For sequence-level sampling methods, such as Best-of-N reranking, the calibrated dual variable corresponds to the solution of the expected-cost constrained problem. For token-level reward-guided decoding methods, the same construction yields a principled dual-calibrated heuristic rather than an exact constrained-policy guarantee. We evaluate LARA on both sequence-level and token-level inference-time alignment methods, and find that LARA improves the helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff, with Best-of-N achieving the best performance among inference-time methods, approaching finetuning-based direct alignment baselines.

item.title: Frozen Factor or Spectral Band? In LoRA, the Factor Matters More at Low Rank [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.06621v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On two main task-model pairs, at ranks 1 to 8 with few optimiser steps, the factor a LoRA variant freezes matters more than its band of singular directions. MiCA and PiCa are compared by band, minor against dominant, yet MiCA freezes the output factor B and PiCa, in our notation, the input factor A. We cross factor and band in a 2 x 2 design on models from 1B to 8B parameters. Freezing A beats freezing B on both bands, by +12 to +20 points at rank 2 on a format task, our primary evidence, and still by about +7 points at rank 8 on OpenBookQA. A Holm correction over 258 primary tests, added post hoc, keeps this advantage in 15 of 16 tests and the lead of factor over band at ranks 1, 2 and 4, rank 1 of the format task being itself post hoc. At rank 8 that lead passes its own test but not the correction. The advantage repeats at rank 2 with two 7B models, by +11 to +13 points. Outside the correction, it repeats on GSM8K with a 1B model and, in a post hoc experiment, with an 8B model at ranks 8 and 16. It holds when B frozen gets as many parameters or more, with a random frozen A, and with sixteen times the format-task budget. It narrows above rank 8 on most pairs, at rank 8 with the 8B model on the two main tasks, on ARC and in a task mixture, and it closes at the last step of longer training on OpenBookQA. At MiCA's and PiCa's own settings, it is smaller or not detected.

item.title: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.21240v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Presenting the same request with different context or formatting can change which sparse autoencoder (SAE) features respond inside a language model. Understanding these changes raises two questions. Which feature responses recur across related inputs, and which of them contribute to downstream computation? We study this phenomenon as representation redistribution and introduce the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS) to identify large feature changes that recur in a consistent direction. We select features on one set of prompt variants and evaluate them on separate variants. Across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, RSS reveals a consistent pattern of redistribution. Context and wrapper transformations produce stronger recurring responses than local edits. We then use two frozen safety readouts to measure how these changes contribute to downstream computation. RSS identifies features with approximately twice the mean held out contribution of features selected by the largest readout coefficients, using activation responses alone. An exact decomposition explains how feature changes and readout coefficients determine their effects on the decision margin. Combining RSS contributions with the clean margin improves recurrent failure AUROC from 0.863 to 0.935 and from 0.901 to 0.958, approaching the full readout results of 0.965 and 0.964. These findings show that recurring changes in sparse representations provide a way to identify features with meaningful downstream contributions. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/Redistribution-Sensitivity-Score.

item.title: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.21261v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide features that can be combined to explain and steer language model behavior. Understanding these combinations requires knowing how reliably individual feature effects predict their joint impact on the model. We study this relationship by retaining or removing subsets of SAE feature contributions and measuring the resulting behavioral responses. We introduce SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR) to quantify how much behavioral variation is explained by feature interactions beyond a chosen order. We prove that, under independent feature subset sampling, SAR measures the normalized energy of these interactions and bounds errors in ranking feature combinations. Across 18 model and behavior settings, learned SAE coordinates have lower first order residuals than matched rotations of the same activation subspace. This shows that SAE coordinates support comparatively simple descriptions of joint feature effects. Pairwise modeling further improves the ranking of held out feature combinations in all 18 settings. We also demonstrate the practical value of modeling these interactions. Across five challenging benchmarks, pairwise models select feature combinations that give higher probability to the correct answer and preserve the original behavioral response more closely than first order models. In MMLU-Pro steering, pairwise modeling improves rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 and reduces ordering error from 0.1444 to 0.0606. These results establish behavioral compositionality as a measurable property of SAE representations and show how modeling feature interactions improves the analysis and selection of feature combinations.
